https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/10/hank.text: Menü Kereső Lemondóan bólogatott Hankó Balázs, amikor Magyar Péter az esetleges kihallgatásáról beszélt Belföld Legfontosabb Hankó Balázs a parlament 2026. augusztus 10-i ülésén – Forrás: Országgyűlés Élő / YouTube Vorák Anita Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Érdekesen reagált Hankó Balázs fideszes képviselő, amikor egy pillanatra váratlanul reflektorfénybe került, miközben Magyar Péter a Mi Hazánk frakcióvezetőjének napirend előtti felszólalására válaszolt a parlamentben. Toroczkai László napirend előtt arról beszélt, hogy a Mi Hazánk megszavazta a Nemzeti Vagyonvisszaszerzési és Vagyonvédelmi Hivatal felállításáról szóló javaslatot, de egyre kevésbé tudnak bízni a miniszterelnökben, mert minden nap bizonyítja, hogy hajlandó visszaélni a hatalmával. Magyar Péter erre reagálva azt mondta Toroczkainak, hogy ha nem szeretné, hogy fideszes politikusokat hallgassanak ki, akkor inkább mondja azt. Majd szóba hozta a Toroczkaitól nem messze ülő Hankó Balázst is, mintha Toroczkai félne, hogy „nehogy esetleg kihallgatásra kerüljön”. Magyar azt mondta, szerinte rendben van, hogy a volt kulturális miniszter volt kabinetfőnökét és minden közeli emberét bevitték, mint ahogy szerinte az sem lesz probléma, ha a Nemzeti Vagyonvisszaszerzési és Vagyonvédelmi Hivatal később kihallgat majd politikusokat is. Eközben a parlamenti közvetítésben már Toroczkait és a tőle balra ülő Hankó Balázst mutatták. Utóbbi grimaszolva, lemondóan bólintva hallgatta Magyar Pétert. https://www.ksmu.org/news/2026-07-28/far.text: On Air Now Playing KSMU HD1 News Farmata brings intimate classical concerts, food and rural hospitality to Fair Grove KSMU | By Jimmy Rea Published July 28, 2026 at 10:55 AM CDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Listen • 35:58 Farmata A rebuilt barn, world-class musicians and farm-to-table hospitality come together at Farmata, where a new concert series offers an intimate listening experience near Fair Grove. A new concert series near Fair Grove is combining world-class classical music with farm-grown food, sustainable living and the intimacy of a house concert. Farmata was created by cellist Steuart Pincombe and his wife, Michelle, on the rural property where they have spent the past seven years developing a homestead. The couple raises hogs, goats, ducks, geese and bees, along with elderberries, fruit trees and other crops. At the center of the project is a rebuilt barn that now hosts concerts for about 20 to 25 people. “It’s basically an invitation into our lives,” Steuart Pincombe said. “Our aim is to pull people into natural beauty, both in what I do in music and what my colleagues do, and in how we try to cultivate the land.” The Pincombe's previously lived in The Hague in the Netherlands, where Steuart performed and taught music. After returning to the United States, they began looking for a place where they could afford land, grow food, raise animals and live closer to family. They eventually settled near Fair Grove, where Steuart's parents live. The concert series developed gradually as Steuart renovated the barn, initially intending to use part of it as a teaching studio. As the space took shape, the couple began imagining small concerts inspired by intimate performances they had experienced in Europe. “We really want to be investing in the place where we live,” Michelle Pincombe said. “We moved here to try to set down roots, contribute to where we are living and celebrate what is unique about rural Missouri.” Food is included with each concert and often highlights ingredients raised on the farm or produced by neighboring farms. For the upcoming performances, Michelle plans to serve homemade Sicilian-style gelato flavored with elderberry, blackberry and pear, along with locally grown watermelon. Farmata’s next concerts will feature Steuart Pincombe on cello and Oregon musician Jonny Rodgers performing on tuned wine glasses. Rodgers adjusts the water level in each glass to change its pitch. The duo’s program will combine guided improvisation, microtonal music and arrangements of works by Estonian composer Arvo Pärt, including "Spiegel im Spiegel" and "Fratres." Microtonal music uses pitches that fall between the notes commonly heard in Western music. Steuart said the duo is approaching the technique gently, creating music intended to soothe rather than unsettle listeners. Audience members will also be invited to participate in one piece using pre-tuned wine glasses while Steuart improvises around the chords they create. The performances will begin at 7 p.m. Aug. 7 and 4 p.m. Aug. 8. Both concerts will feature the same general program, although the improvisational elements will make each performance different. Tickets and additional information are available through Farmata’s website at www.farmata.org . News Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Jimmy Rea Jimmy Rea is a proud Ozarkian with deep ties to the music community. With 2 decades of creative entrepreneurship underfoot, Jimmy has toured coast to coast and around the world with acoustic acts The HillBenders and Keller Williams. Spearheading numerous musical groups, recording projects, and live music events, Rea’s work in the Springfield music scene is a passion and lifestyle. Happily married to wife Melissa and father to Archie, they enjoy life together with 2 dogs and a cat. In his downtime you can find Jimmy fishing for bass in the crisp rivers, creeks, and streams of the Ozarks. See stories by Jimmy Rea

https://www.dw.com/en/norway-seizes-russ.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5L0dJ The research vessel was taking a group of researchers to Barentsburg, a Russian coal mining settlement on the Arctic Svalbard archipelago Image: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance Advertisement Norwegian courts have ordered the seizure of a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce part of a $4.22 billion (roughly €3.6 billion) compensation claim won by Ukrainian state energy firm Naftogaz after Moscow's seizure of its assets in Crimea , which Russia illegally annexed in 2014. Officials announced that the ship had been stopped from departing the port in the Russian coal mining settlement of Barentsburg in the Svalbard archipelago late on Wednesday. Svalbard has been Norwegian territory since 1925 but is a demilitarized zone where people from dozens of countries, Russia included, can settle without visas under certain conditions. Russia's ambassador to Norway said that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels. Around two thirds of Svalbard is designated as national parks and nature reserves, but the coal mining settlement of Barentsburg is home to about a tenth of the archipelago's population Image: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance What do we know about the Professor Molchanov ship being impounded? The first group to announce the ship's seizure was Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz as it tries to secure the compensation awarded to it by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague in 2023. Russia had refused to pay the fine plus legal fees and interest amid its ongoing war with Ukraine , and Naftogaz has since begun trying to secure the seizure and forced sale of Russian commercial assets via local courts instead. "Russia cannot evade ​responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," said Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko. Covington said it had been tracking the ship, the Professor Molchanov , for months. It said its application was approved on Monday by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court, which ordered Svalbard's governor to ensure the ship stayed in dock once it arrived. The end of coal mining in Svalbard To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The Svalbard governor's office later issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held in Svalbard. "The governor will take care of the crew and passengers on board the vessel in collaboration with Trust Arktikugol," it said, referring to the Russian enterprise (meaning "Arctic Coal") that administers the Barentsburg mining settlement. Norway's Justice Ministry, meanwhile, said the issue did not directly concern the government in Oslo. "Russia can demand that ​the district court reassess the case," the Justice ‌Ministry said. How did Russia respond? Russia's ambassador to Norway, Nikolai Korchunov, said in a statement on Thursday that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels. "We insist on the immediate release of the vessel and on ensuring the safety of its passengers and crew," he said. The Kremlin also summoned Norway's ambassador in Moscow to lodge a formal complaint. Is Svalbard Russia's real leverage in the Arctic? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The Professor Molchanov , a repurposed research vessel, arrived in Barentsburg on Tuesday with a party of Russian scientists, according to a journalist who was accompanying them. "The seizure has had no impact on the expedition participants or the ship's crew. No one has been arrested. We are all going about our business as usual," Andrei Gorbunov, editor-in-chief of Komsomolskaya Pravda (KP) radio wrote on KP's website. He said that for the time being, "the Professor Mochanov is simply forbidden from leaving the port of Barentsburg," adding it was unclear how long this would remain the case. Prior to the war in Ukraine Barentsburg was also home to Ukrainian and other foreign nationals. But most have since left, Ukrainians in particular were told to accept an offer of Russian citizenship or leave. Image: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance What is behind Svalbard's special status, and why is it home to the Barentsburg settlement? Svalbard is an archipelago well to the north of mainland Norway in the Arctic Circle, sparsely populated and thought to be home to slightly fewer than 3,000 people. It was a whaling base in the 17th and 18th centuries and became a coal mining site at the beginning of the 20th century. The territory was recognized as part of Norway in 1925, but only after the 1920 establishment of an international treaty — which nowadays has dozens of signatories — designating the area a demilitarized zone where anybody from a signatory state was permitted to settle and work without a visa , provided they met certain conditions. The Soviet Union eventually acquired three sites and developed them as company towns: Barentsburg, with a remnant population of around 300 mostly Russian nationals, the nearly-abandoned settlement of Pyramiden, and Grumant, which has been left as a ghost town for decades. Tourism has become a growth industry on the stark but stunning polar archipelago. https://www.dw.com/en/a-romani-artist-in.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MVpi Roma artist Norbert Olah in the Bura Galeria in Budapest Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW Advertisement The painting on the canvas is of a man playing chess with a robot. The color on his face is still damp and glistening. Norbert Olah was working into the early hours: The Bura Galeria in Budapest has been his studio all summer. He finds it easiest to concentrate at night, when the Hungarian capital gradually falls silent. Olah has taped foil and cardboard over the tiled floor at the back of the gallery. Pots of brushes, tubes of paint, pencil sketches, and, over and over again, pictures that include the blue-and-green Roma flag line the room. Norbert Olah is an artist. He's also Romani. For a long time, he deliberately left this part of his identity out of his art. Not because his ethnicity wasn't important to him, but because he didn't want to be labeled a "Romani artist." "There are so many prejudices about Roma culture and Roma art," Olah says. "The art scene regards it as naïve, unprofessional, unsophisticated, and kitsch." But the older Olah got, the harder he found it to ignore his own story in his art. Especially in a country in which being Romani is not just an ethnicity but a political reality. Life under Orban The first time Viktor Orban 's Fidesz party won an absolute majority in the Hungarian parliamentary elections of 2010, Olah had just finished school and was starting his art course at the Hungarian University of Fine Arts in Budapest. At a time of life when the world ought to be opening up, Olah felt more and more barriers were being erected. Norbert Olah with his paintings: The Bura Galeria is a platform for contemporary Roma art Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW Olah was directly affected by Hungary 's political reorientation, as both an artist and a Romani. Politics co-opted the cultural scene and made it toe the party line. Roma became the target of hateful rhetoric, including from the prime minister himself. Orban repeatedly called attention to himself with racist comments about Roma. For the 16 years Orban was in power, Hungary's Roma population, estimated to be around 700,000 people, was caught between official promises of integration and persistent marginalization. Orban's government introduced a state employment program that hired predominantly Romani workers. But instead of helping them gain a foothold in the job market, many Romani found themselves trapped in insecure, poorly paid, temporary jobs. The government did little to implement real change. Romani in Hungary are still disproportionately affected by poverty and social exclusion. There came a point when Norbert Olah felt he could no longer stand by and do nothing. Other people's prejudices In 2021, during Hungary's biggest independent contemporary art event, the OFF-Biennale Budapest , Olah and his father laid a brick wall directly in front of the entrance to the building that had housed the Roma Parliament , a Roma cultural center with an art collection, archive, library, and events program. The Orban government evicted it in 2016, saying the building was structurally dangerous and promising to repurpose it as a national Roma center. It has stood empty ever since. The title of Olah's work was "The Romani Artist's Fears." Words like "integration," "assimilation," and "segregation" were chiseled into the bricks. A few weeks later, Olah staged a performance in which he took a sledgehammer to his artwork and smashed it till it collapsed. In an accompanying text, Olah wrote publicly for the first time about the fears, prejudices, and expectations he encounters as an artist with Roma roots. The text is full of questions. Should a Romani artist's work focus on topics relevant to Roma? What is the relationship between ethnicity and aesthetics? Would people only contact an artist with Roma roots if they were specifically looking for a Romani artist, or would they do so if they needed a Hungarian artist, too? Roma on the moon: Olah's current project looks to the future Image: Norbert Oláh "Of course we're always looking for answers. But sometimes it's more interesting to look at the question itself," says Olah, picking a piece of crepe masking tape off the floor. "If it feels uncomfortable, it's a good question." And so Olah has created a new label for Romani artists. The Bura Galeria, established by Romani activists in 2021 in Budapest's District 8, has become the place for it: A platform for contemporary Roma art. "We're not asking to be accepted by the art scene," said Olah. "We're opening the door and inviting others in." Open antiziganism Identity and exclusion, power and the misuse of power — these became central themes for Olah's artistic work. He had no lack of inspiration during the Orban years. Although Fidesz's policies were hardly favorable to Roma, Orban's party could, for a long time, count on Roma votes — for example, because local employment programs enabled local politicians to pressure socially underprivileged voters. There were also many documented cases of vote-buying. Fidesz was so confident that the majority of Roma would continue to vote for it that it openly fueled the antiziganism still widespread in Hungarian society. After Orban, Hungary's Roma hope for change To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Shortly before the election in April 2026, Fidesz's Janos Lazar, who was minister for transport at the time, spoke out against labor migration with the argument that Hungary still had "domestic reserves," like the Roma, who could "clean the crap out of overflowing toilets" on Intercity trains. The scene appears in Olah's art: A fake election poster depicts a man in a balaclava sitting on a golden toilet, brandishing a toilet brush, with the slogan underneath: "Gypsy Criminals for President." Opportunity for real change? Gypsy Criminals is also the name of the artists' collective Olah founded in 2024, along with a friend of his and his miniature pinscher. The term comes from Hungarian crime statistics, and has been used since the 2000s by right-wing politicians to imply that all Roma are criminals. The name is ironic, like many aspects of Olah's work. Analyses by the foundation Roma for Democracy show that many Roma did not vote for Orban's Fidesz party in the April 2026 parliamentary election. Orban's successor, Peter Magyar, adopted a different tone in relation to Roma as part of his election campaign. He met with members of the Roma minority, and his election manifesto contained a specific paragraph about equal opportunities for Roma . Four of the Tisza party's nine new members of parliament are Romani. One was even elected a deputy speaker of parliament. Since the election, there has been cautious optimism that the precarious situation of many Roma in Hungary could finally change. On the other hand, nothing has fundamentally changed in the four months since the election, apart from the tone when talking about the ethnic minority. "What I'm seeing right now are mostly symbolic gestures," says Olah. Roma on Mars Some of his friends in the more liberal art scene are growing impatient. They would like to see Magyar take a much more liberal course, but Olah is a realist. "He's a conservative politician," he says. "We elected him to put an end to the Orban system. He didn't promise any more than that." But the election in April was an opportunity for a fresh political start, he adds. "I think in the long run we will live in a normal society again, led by a normal government, that will do some things well and others not so well. As an artist, it will be my job to criticize that." Man v. robot: Olah works on a new painting in his Budapest studio Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW Olah's work also considers the future. The first pictures for his next project are already up on the wall in his studio. It's Roma futurism: A Romani couple strolling on Mars; a blue-and-green Roma flag on the moon; a weightless astronaut with a traditional Cegled water jug, used by Romani musicians as a percussion instrument. Olah is also planning a two-meter-high space station in the shape of a cartwheel, a symbol of the Romani people. For Olah, space travel is also a metaphor for social advancement — the desire of people and communities to overcome the barriers they face as a result of their origins, or poverty, or life in a minority. Again, he is asking questions. What if a society were fundamentally recreated from the beginning? If aliens encountered Roma, would they do so without prejudice? What remains of an identity if everything about it changes? Olah shreds the masking tape between his fingers. More unanswered questions. But that's exactly what makes them so interesting. https://telex.hu/gazdasag/2026/09/29/egy.text: Menü Kereső Érdemben kevesebb az egyajánlatos közbeszerzés a kormányváltás óta Gazdaság Weiler Vilmos Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom A kormányváltás utáni szerda, vagyis május 13. óta 22,1 százalékról 17,4 százalékra csökkent az egyajánlatos közbeszerzések aránya Magyarországon – közölte a kormány kedden . Ezzel érdemben közelebb kerültünk az Európai Unió által kitűzött 15 százalékos célhoz. Magyarországon hosszú ideje komoly probléma, hogy az állami szervek által kiírt közbeszerzések feltűnően nagy részén csak egyetlen cég tesz érvényes ajánlatot. Ezt az Európai Unió is kifogásolja, ami miatt még az előző kormány vállalta, hogy 2024-re 15 százalék alá csökkenti ezek arányát. Ez nem jött össze, az új kormány azonban az uniós források elérése érdekében meg akarja valósítani az előző kormány vállalását. A céljuk továbbra is az, hogy a nagyobb állami közbeszerzések kevesebb mint 15 százalékát bonyolítsák le úgy, hogy arra csak egy ajánlat érkezik. A Miniszterelnökség most megnézte, hogy a 2026. január elseje és szeptember 10-e között aláírt közbeszerzési szerződéseknél hány ajánlattevő volt. Az év első kétharmadát két részre bontották: a kormányalakítás előtti, január és május 12. közötti időszakot; a kormányalakítás utáni, május 13. és szeptember 10. közötti időszakot. A kimutatásuk szerint az előbbiben 22,1, az utóbbiban 17,4 százalék volt az egyajánlatos beszerzések aránya, az tehát a kormányváltás után érdemben csökkent. Még látványosabb a változás a jellemzően nagyobb értékű keretmegállapodásoknál, amelyeknél ez az arány 44,4 százalékról 27 százalékra csökkent. A kormány közleménye szerint a több ajánlat azzal jár együtt, hogy az állam könnyebben válogathat a cégek között és olcsóbban jut hozzá jobb termékekhez és szolgáltatásokhoz. https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2026/10.text: Menu Search Latest Profile English Contact | About | International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Menu Search International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Latest Profile Fourth International Socialist Equality Party IYSSE About the WSWS Contact Donate For the first time in history, the Trotskyist movement is standing a candidate in a New Zealand general election. The Socialist Equality Group (SEG) is fielding Tom Petterson because the working class confronts a crisis of historic proportions, and because no party contesting this election offers it any way forward. Our campaign is not a bid for office within the existing order. It is an intervention to expose the bankruptcy of every party of the capitalist establishment, and to raise the necessity of a socialist and internationalist leadership of the working class. We call on workers and young people to support this campaign, and to register to attend our public meeting on November 1, at 1:30 p.m. in the Dowse Art Museum (James Coe Centre), 45 Laings Road, Lower Hutt. This election is taking place as world capitalism enters the most dangerous period since the Second World War. The economic crisis that erupted in 2008 was never resolved and has intensified following the COVID-19 pandemic. The ruling classes of every country have responded with a relentless assault on the living standards of working people, the promotion of far-right and fascist forces, and the drive to violently redivide the world. The fronts of a third world war are opening before our eyes: the US-NATO war against Russia in Ukraine, the genocide in Gaza, the criminal and expanding war against Iran, the seizure of Venezuelan oil and the militarisation of the entire Indo-Pacific in preparation for war against China. The danger of nuclear war is a real and present one. At the same time, the working class is fighting back. Mass strikes and demonstrations by youth and school students have erupted in France, millions are protesting against the housing crisis in Spain, and strikes are unfolding across the United States and throughout the world. New Zealand is no exception: Last October more than 100,000 teachers and healthcare workers took part in the country’s biggest strike in nearly 50 years against the government’s attacks on wages and conditions—a struggle which was strangled by the union apparatus. What is lacking is not the capacity of the working class to fight, but a leadership with the program necessary to unify workers internationally against the source of austerity and war. The trade union bureaucracies, the social-democratic parties and the pseudo-left “socialist” groups all function to subordinate the class struggle to the interests of the bourgeoisie. The building of a new, revolutionary leadership is the central question of the epoch. New Zealand: A minor imperialist power New Zealand presents itself to the world as a kinder, gentler capitalism, a model of egalitarianism and decency. This is a fraud. New Zealand is a minor imperialist power, which, together with Australia, seeks to corral the Pacific Island nations behind the war drive of US imperialism against China. Successive Labour and National-led governments have called for the New Zealand military to be made “combat-ready” to join a US-led war far beyond its territory. Wellington and Canberra have agreed to uphold the ANZUS Treaty, which would automatically drag both countries into a US war against China. The Pacific, which experienced some of the most devastating battles of World War II, is again being turned into a staging ground for imperialist war. Within New Zealand, the ruling class presides over some of the sharpest levels of inequality in the developed world. One in five children lives in poverty, 10 percent of people rely on foodbanks to survive and more than 112,000 people are homeless. While workers’ real wages have plummeted by 6.4 percent since 2021, the number of billionaires has doubled in the past eight years and the size of their fortunes has grown enormously. The National Business Review Rich List now records more than $129 billion in the hands of just 150 individuals and families—more than a quarter of the country’s annual GDP. This is not an accident of policy. It is the product of the capitalist system itself, which can only enrich the few by impoverishing the many. We say: No money for war! End all military spending and redirect billions of dollars to schools, hospitals and ending poverty. Withdraw from the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing network and close the Waihopai spy base. Abolish the intelligence agencies. Abolish the ANZUS Treaty and end all military alliances and agreements with the US, Australia, NATO and elsewhere. Withdraw all New Zealand troops from the Middle East, Europe and every overseas deployment. Labour and National: Two parties of war and austerity Governments led by National and Labour have supported US imperialism at every turn. The current National-led coalition has deployed military personnel to the Middle East to assist the US attacks in Yemen and in keeping supply lines open for Israel’s war machine. The previous Labour-led government sent New Zealand troops to train Ukrainian conscripts in Britain to fight in Russia—a deployment that has since been expanded to Poland as the war escalates and threatens the use of nuclear weapons. Labour agrees with National that military spending must increase dramatically—from 1 to at least 2 percent of GDP—and that recruitment must expand. This will be funded by starving healthcare, education and other vital public services. This election will resolve nothing. All the political parties contesting it—Labour, National, and all their support parties—are committed to defending capitalism, which requires a deepening assault on the working class and the integration of the country into US imperialism’s war plans. The differences between the parties are minor and tactical. A vote for any of them is a vote for austerity and for war. The previous Labour-led government, under Prime Ministers Jacinda Ardern and Chris Hipkins, is directly responsible for the coming to power in 2023 of the right-wing coalition of National, ACT and NZ First. In 2017 Ardern formed a coalition with the Greens and the right-wing nationalist NZ First, appointing its leader Winston Peters as deputy prime minister and foreign minister. It was the Ardern government’s attacks on living standards, anti-immigrant measures and strengthening of military ties with Washington, which prepared the ground for the current right-wing government. Ardern’s promises in 2017 to address poverty and inequality were a fraud: Under her government, homelessness and the number of children living in material hardship increased. The working class turned against Labour, which lost the 2023 election in a landslide, as real wages plummeted and as the government dismantled public health protections against COVID-19, leading to a surge in hospitalisation and death. The Labour Party ditched any attachment to reformist policies during the 1980s government of Prime Minister David Lange and Finance Minister Roger Douglas, which carried out a brutal assault on the working class, similar to that by Reagan in the US and Thatcher in Britain. It responded to the globalisation of production by privatising industries, removing state subsidies, sacking tens of thousands of workers, and slashing taxes for the rich. All these attacks were enforced by the Stalinist-led union bureaucracy. The result was soaring social inequality and unemployment—a social disaster that continues to this day. After decades of right-wing attacks, Labour and National are both widely despised: Their combined support has fallen to less than 60 percent, the lowest level since the 1930s. This mirrors the collapse in support for social-democratic parties internationally, including in France, Britain and Spain, and represents a serious crisis of rule for the bourgeoisie that has relied on these parties to contain and suppress the class struggle. To return to power, the Labour Party will have to form a coalition with two or three minor parties, and will rely heavily on the support of middle-class, pseudo-left groups. To defend living standards, we call for: An immediate 20 percent pay increase for all workers, and a rise in all benefits, to reverse years of real wage cuts. Index all wages and benefits to the cost of living, with automatic monthly adjustments. A full-time, permanent job on decent wages for all who want one; a living income for those unable to work. Cancel student debt and restore free tertiary education. Free, universal healthcare; reverse the slashing of health and education workers’ wages and the sacking of thousands of public servants. To carry out a real struggle against wage cuts, job losses and the militarisation of society, workers must rebel against the trade union bureaucracy. The unions ceased to be workers’ organisations decades ago and now function as an industrial police force for the state and big business. Workers must build rank-and-file committees, democratically controlled and independent of the union apparatus and the capitalist parties. These committees must unite workers in New Zealand across all industries and with workers in Australia, Asia, the Pacific and throughout the world, through the International Workers’ Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees. The Greens, Te Pāti Māori and the Opportunity Party The Green Party and the Māori nationalist Te Pāti Māori (TPM) are positioning themselves to provide a “progressive” veneer for a right-wing government led by Labour. Both parties will ditch their meagre reform proposals—including calls for the rich to pay more tax and for measures to improve “affordability”—the second they enter a coalition with Labour. In the Ardern government, the Greens loyally backed Labour’s budgets, which boosted military spending while starving education, healthcare and other services. TPM was part of the 2008–2017 National Party-led government which increased GST, slashed welfare entitlements and partially privatised electricity companies. Socialism AI by the WSWS SocialismAI.com Questions about this article? Ask Socialism AI What is the historical origin and purpose of the International Committee of the Fourth International, and how does it differ from other groups that call themselves socialist or Trotskyist? Can you explain the Labour government's 1980s 'Rogernomics' reforms in New Zealand and how they compare to Reaganism and Thatcherism elsewhere? How did the Stalinist-led union bureaucracies historically come to suppress class struggle, and what does that history explain about the role of unions in New Zealand today? Ask more questions at SocialismAI.com The Greens and TPM, along with the pseudo-lefts, promote reactionary forms of identity politics based on nationality, race and gender, which divides the working class and obscures the most important division in society: the gulf between workers and capitalists. TPM speaks for Māori tribal-based capitalists seeking a greater share of the wealth extracted from the working class. Their interests are opposed to those of Māori workers, who are among the most exploited in the country. The Opportunity Party (TOP), which says it could work with either Labour or National, could hold the balance of power and choose which of the main parties leads the next government. TOP, which has not been in parliament before, claims to be “pragmatic” and “centrist.” In fact it is a right-wing, pro-business party which, like the Greens, peddles the fraud that climate change, the housing crisis and soaring living costs can all be resolved within the capitalist market system. Unite the working class Reject identity politics and the parties that peddle it. The fight against racism and all oppression requires the unity of workers across ethnic, gender and national divisions—not their subordination to competing sections of the capitalist elite. Defend immigrants—full citizenship rights for all; end the deportations and repeal all anti-immigrant measures. The role of the pseudo-left The pseudo-left groups, particularly the International Socialist Organisation (ISO) and Socialist Aotearoa (SA), play a key role in enabling Labour’s betrayals. Both groups whitewashed the right-wing Ardern government as “reformist” and are again calling on workers and youth to vote for Labour or its allied parties, based on the lie that they are a “lesser evil” or even a progressive alternative to National. In response to the war against Iran, SA and the ISO both called for an “anti-war” alliance with the pro-imperialist Labour and Green parties. The ISO and SA are not socialist organisations but nationalist groups operating within the political establishment and the union bureaucracy to disarm workers and subordinate them to parties of big business and war. The pseudo-lefts speak for affluent middle-class layers whose privileged position rests on New Zealand’s role as a US-allied imperialist power. A socialist program of action The demands we have set out cannot be won through appeals to the capitalist state but pose the need for a political fight against it. Every one of them collides with the profit system and the parties that defend it. The fight for them therefore raises, at every point, the question of which class holds power. The wealth of the country—including the $129 billion in the hands of 150 families and the $39.5 billion in bank profits between 2020 and 2025—was created by the working class and must be taken back. The banks and major corporations must be nationalised under the democratic control of the working class, and the wealth of the billionaires seized. This requires the working class to take political power—to break up the existing state machine and establish a workers’ government that will reorganise society to meet human need. What the working class lacks is not the capacity to fight, but a revolutionary leadership. The building of that leadership—the New Zealand section of the International Committee of the Fourth International, the world party of socialist revolution founded by Leon Trotsky—is the central task. Photograph: Alex Wroblewski/AFP/Getty Images US news Retired Michigan teacher released from Russian prison believed he would never be freed Stephen Hubbard said that only when he was being taken from Moscow to St Petersburg did he believe he was ‘going somewhere’ Guardian staff and agencies Fri 30 Oct 2026 19.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In his first comments since recently being released from a Russian prison, a retired Michigan teacher said he only believed he would be freed when he got new clothes. Stephen Hubbard, 74, remarked on Friday that he had heard many times previously that he would be released – but never really trusted what he was told, adopting a philosophy of “seeing is believing” and “actions speak louder than words”. “Only when they started giving me new clothes and leading me to the exit of the prison,” Hubbard said in his first public remarks since his 21 October release, which came during a visit at the White House with Donald Trump , “I went out and I saw the car, and I was accompanied by a couple of Russians, then I believed, finally believed, on the drive from Moscow to St Petersburg, ‘I’m really going somewhere.’” Hubbard had been behind bars for more than four years on charges that he fought as a mercenary in Ukraine , which Russia invaded in February 2022. His legal team has denied the Russian accusations and said he was not involved in any military activity. Trump has previously said that he had asked Russian leader Vladimir Putin to free Hubbard – and that the US did not have to release anyone in return. “He was somebody I wanted to get back,” the US president said as he hosted Hubbard on Friday in the Oval Office. The White House allowed a limited pool of journalists into Trump’s meeting with Hubbard, allowing primarily news photographers and a television crew. Many in the international community perceived Hubbard’s release to be Russia’s latest maneuver to bring Trump closer to Putin’s position on the war in Ukraine . It also offered Trump a diplomatic victory ahead of the 3 November midterm elections, when his Republican party is expected to lose seats in Congress.
